title: Return to Sport and Physical Activity After Hip Resurfacing Arthroplasty Versus Total Hip Arthroplasty in Young, Active Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
content: Background: Hip resurfacing arthroplasty (HRA) is widely believed to confer a greater capacity for high-level physical activity than total hip arthroplasty (THA) in young, active patients. However, the extent to which this apparent advantage reflects a true procedural effect, as opposed to preferential selection of more active patients for HRA, remains unclear.Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with PRISMA 2020, searching PubMed and Scopus for comparative studies reporting post-operative University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity scores in patients undergoing HRA versus THA. Pooled mean differences (MD) were estimated using a random-effects model (restricted maximum likelihood). Pre-specified subgroup analyses stratified studies by design (comparative versus non-comparative) and by whether baseline activity level was equalised between treatment arms at study entry.Results: Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria (1,327 hips; 644 HRA, 683 THA). Patients undergoing HRA achieved modestly higher post-operative activity scores than those undergoing THA (MD 0.75, 95% CI 0.35–1.14; p<0.001), a difference below the accepted minimal clinically important difference of one point. Heterogeneity was high (I²=78%). Study design category did not explain this heterogeneity (comparative versus non-comparative studies, p=0.69); however, baseline activity equalisation did: studies with unequal baseline activity reported more than double the effect size of those with equalised baselines (1.47 vs 0.51 points; p<0.001). No evidence of publication bias was detected (Egger's p=0.55; Begg's p=0.68).Discussion: The activity advantage attributed to hip resurfacing is small, clinically marginal, and appears substantially attributable to baseline selection of more active patients rather than a true procedural benefit. Future comparative studies of post-operative activity after hip arthroplasty should prospectively match or statistically adjust for baseline activity level to minimise confounding by indication.
